title: AI Giants Face Antitrust Lawsuit Over Alleged Slowdown Agreement
summary:
A new lawsuit filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California claims that Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google made an illegal agreement to slow down their AI development. The suit argues that the companies violated antitrust laws by coordinating slowdown efforts, which would reduce the value consumers get for paid AI subscriptions.

The coordination allegedly took place on September 12, when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay urging industrywide cooperation on decelerating advancements in favor of enhanced safety measures. That same day, OpenAI's Sam Altman, SpaceXAI's Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis each publicly responded in agreement.

The plaintiffs argue that an agreement among chief rivals that their progress "should be slower than competition would otherwise produce has an anticompetitive effect on consumers." Lawyers representing four named plaintiffs, who pay for subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini, are bringing the suit on behalf of a proposed nationwide class of other paid subscribers.

"AI will quickly spin out of human control and could kill us all if we allow AI safety and protocol ... to be controlled by private self-serving agreements between the world's most powerful 'for profit' technology companies," said Nick Rowley, the lead attorney for the plaintiffs.

Representatives for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and SpaceXAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.

In his essay, Amodei acknowledged potential antitrust challenges, writing that it would be helpful for the U.S. government to mediate "or at least enable" these cross-lab discussions. The government wouldn't need to participate, he wrote, but would need to "issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations." Altman responded on social media that OpenAI welcomes a "federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements," but said "we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence."

While the recent conversations about pacing development were spurred by increasing concerns about AI evading human control, several leaders in the AI space have long talked about developing a shared set of standards or otherwise coordinating to ensure safety efforts remained paramount.
why_it_matters: The case asks who gets to decide how quickly AI develops — companies, governments, or courts — and whether saying 'we did it for safety' can legally excuse rivals for agreeing to slow down. A ruling either way would shape the rules for an industry that touches almost everything teenagers use online.

background_read: For more than a century, U.S. law has treated agreements between competitors as dangerous. The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 — the first federal law banning monopolies and cartels — and later the Clayton Act gave the government and private citizens the power to sue companies that work together to control prices or limit what they offer. Historic cases broke up John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil and the phone giant AT&T, and in the late 1990s the Justice Department (the federal department that enforces competition law alongside the FTC, the Federal Trade Commission) sued Microsoft over how it bundled its web browser. The core idea is that rivals agreeing to hold back what they sell hurts consumers even when their motives sound good.

The AI firms named in the suit are among the best known in the field: OpenAI (the company behind ChatGPT), Anthropic (founded by former OpenAI researchers and maker of the Claude chatbot), Google DeepMind (Google's AI research lab), and the AI company the article calls SpaceXAI. Since 2023, AI safety has been a loud public argument inside the industry — thousands of researchers signed an open letter that year calling for a pause on training the largest AI systems, and some warn that advanced AI could become difficult for humans to control. Regulators such as the FTC have also been asking whether the biggest AI companies are absorbing or shutting out smaller rivals.

perspectives.description: If the court sides with the plaintiffs, AI firms could not quietly agree to hold back better or cheaper products, and the case reaffirms that competition, not private deals, decides what customers get. It could also push governments to write clear AI safety rules instead of leaving them to the biggest companies.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the companies and safety researchers
perspectives.description: They would argue that advanced AI carries real risks of slipping out of human control, and that talking about safety across labs is responsible, not criminal. Forcing every lab to compete at full speed with no coordination might make a dangerous release more likely, not less.

Antitrust law has long held that rivals agreeing to limit output is illegal even when their motives sound noble, and this suit applies that classic theory to an unusual claim about a slower product. Everything would hinge on proving that the public statements on September 12 were really an agreement rather than four people saying similar things.

Expect pressure to create a legal 'safe harbour' so companies can discuss safety without breaking competition law, plus new federal AI legislation. Either way, more lawsuits over AI pricing and market power are likely as the technology spreads.
